newsitem.title: COMOROS: Comoran islanders back Anjouan secessionists.
newsitem.headline: Comoran islanders back Anjouan secessionists.

text.p: Comoran security forces on Wednesday dispersed demonstrators on the Indian Ocean island of Moheli protesting in support of secessionists on the island of Anjouan, witnesses said.

In Ethiopia, the Organisation of African Unity named Ivory Coast Ambassador Pierre Yere as its special envoy to Comoros and said he would leave next weekend for talks with the government and secessionists.
France welcomed with relief the decision by the OAU to mediate between the government of Comoros and the secessionists demanding a return to French rule.
French Foreign Ministry spokesman Yves Doutriaux said the OAU's decision, which Paris had called for, testified to the continent's growing desire to head off conflicts through diplomacy.

"We rejoice that the OAU has decided to appoint a special envoy to the Comoros, as Comorian authorities had called for, in order to help this country find a lasting solution to the crisis born from the situation on the island of Anjouan, " he said.
Witnesses said supporters of separation of Moheli from the Federal Islamic Republic of the Comoros took to the streets of the Moheli capital Fomboni, building barricades and burning tyres.

They raised the French flag on government buildings including the law courts before being dispersed by security forces. Moheli is the smallest of the three islands in the Comoro archipelago and has a population of some 25,000.
The Comoro Islands, which has some 670,000 people, became independent from France in 1975.

Secessionists say that the main island of Grande Comore has been favoured over other islands, and independence has brought only poverty to the island group, in contrast with the relative prosperity of Mayotte, the archipelago's only island which voted to remain French in a 1975 referendum on independence.

The OAU said in a statement its envoy would discuss measures to defuse tension "while addressing the legitimate concerns of the islanders while maintaining the unity, territorial integrity and cohesion" of Comoros.
A committee campaigning for the autonomy of Moheli said on Wednesday it supported the struggle of the people of Anjouan for self-determination and condemned violence by security forces.
The commmittee called on the OAU to hold a referendum on self-determination for Moheli and demanded the withdrawal of security forces from Anjouan.
Secessionists on Anjouan said on Tuesday they had elected their 75-year-old leader Foundi Abdallah Ibrahim as "president" of their breakaway state and feared troops on the island would intervene.
They told a news conference in the Anjouan capital of Mutsamudu that Fatima Abdere Mahe was appointed deputy president and Charikane Ahmed was put in charge of coordination with the president.
Former Comoran prime minister Mohamed Abdou Madi, 41, was appointed foreign minister for the new state of Anjouan.

Ibrahim, who has worked as both a Koranic teacher and a jeweller, was arrested by authorities for five days last month. He and three other secessionist leaders were freed after troops fired on demonstrators.
Anjouan's poverty contrasts with the relative prosperity of the island of Mayotte, which voted to remain French in 1975.
France has denounced the secessionists, saying the Anjouan situation is serious and could destabilise the whole region.
Comoran President Mohamed Taki said last week the islands would be given more autonomy and would be divided into communes.

Three people including a gendarme were killed on July 14 as demonstrators pressing for Anjouan to return to French rule or be independent clashed with security forces. Several were killed in March clashes.
